runners: the say-back: the viewer never speaks; the host turns to the camera, holds as if we had spoken, and says our question aloud, three times (Does it help? / What if none of it ever gets put right? / Should you come up?)

other ways of talking with a silent viewer: a yes taken in a pause (Good. Let me get my scarf.), a question asked of us and an unheard answer agreed with (So. How have you been? / Yeah. Me too.), a look answered with nothing repeated (No cars, I know. I wait anyway.), a glance to see whether we heard what he let slip
two sets of footsteps, the host's and the viewer's, a little out of step, stopping whenever we stop; the only sound the viewer makes, and the only sound under the line of the poem
things going dark and warm light found: the logo goes out, the work lamp clicks off, lit glass is seen from the cold twice, and at the end a door opens and warm light falls across the snow
outside lit glass looking in at people who are warm: a restaurant window, then the same picture smaller as the top window over the host's own door, then we are inside it
one sentence for the good and the bad, then handed to the people in the old books with its person changed: I keep saying, I can't believe it / They couldn't believe it, either
good and bad together, said in the first minute and again in the owner's closing line: The good way and the bad way. Same hour. / It's a crazy mixed up world out there
something the host has by heart at each end of the walk: a sentence he keeps saying, then one line of an old poem he walks the last block with

a warm thing said through an old text, then a dry line of the host's own to get out from under it, twice within twenty seconds: the poem and That's the poem talking. Mostly.; the couplet and So you see my position.
the host by himself, three lines, then answered: I usually walk this block on my own / Just me / They'll have started without me, then Nobody has started and I had company
glad of company, said through a poem to the viewer and then plainly to his friends: Rich did I feel when a comrade I found / I had company / Keep the ones that make you feel sane close
the word guest three times, never remarked on: I'm a guest in that sentence / you don't eat while a guest stands outside / The guest is served first
not eating until the guest is in: told as an old couplet at the door, then done by the house (Nobody has started; every plate clean)
not finishing: a busker's tune that stops one note short, He never does get to the end of it, then a quoted sentence about not having to complete the work, then We don't have to finish it
small words that return: anyway (He'd started anyway / I wait anyway) and started (He'd started anyway / They'll have started without me / Nobody has started)
old texts, four of them, and the word old said of each: So I've been reading old books. Very old. / an old Chinese book / a used book / an old Norse poem / an old Tamil book of couplets
tellings marked as tellings: The way I remember it / Here's how I borrow it / As I remember it / I'm probably saying that wrong; of the poem he claims only one line
short dry tags that end the host's thoughts: Same hour. / I looked. / Some nights. / Still sharp. / Mostly.
the host's habits: I keep saying / I like the walk home / I always stop here / I wait anyway / I usually walk this block on my own / He never does get to the end of it
waiting: he waits for a sign on an empty road, the sign stays red after he has said his piece, six friends have waited for him, the door is opened before he can ask
the rule, used against the host in his own house: That is the rule / It's my house / It's still the rule / And the ruling stands!

things that move with no hand, because nobody has hands: a coin, a street door, a second chair, a place setting; a scarf, a dish's lid and a served bowl change at a cut, and nothing slides along the table
one family of small dry click doing five jobs: a sign's flicker as its power fails, a lamp switched off, a coin landing, a pedestrian sign changing, a door's latch
gold as a marker of what is the host's, with no line pointing at it: his scarf, the chair kept empty for him
a blank pay envelope: leaning on the host's mug, then at his coat pocket until he sits down to eat
catchphrases: Oh, no show tonight, folks. Holidays and all. (the owner's line; the first words, with no title or announcer before them)
Just here picking up my paycheck. (the owner's line) / They'd mail it. I like the walk home.
Would you walk with me a bit? (the owner's line) / Good. Let me get my scarf.
So. How have you been? / Yeah. Me too.
I keep saying, "I can't believe it." / The good way and the bad way. Same hour.
I don't have a joke for that. / I looked.
So I've been reading old books. Very old. / They couldn't believe it, either. Some wrote down what helped.
Does it help? / Some nights.
I always stop here. / One cook in back, feeding the whole room.
The Zhuangzi. I'm probably saying that wrong.
When he comes to a hard part, he slows down. / Looks right at it. Goes gently.
That's a good one. Thank you.
Nobody there till we came by. He'd started anyway.
He never does get to the end of it.
No cars, I know. I wait anyway.
What if none of it ever gets put right? / I don't know. I really don't.
It is not thy duty to complete the work, but neither art thou free to desist from it. (Rabbi Tarfon, Pirkei Avot, in Gorfinkle's translation; quoted exactly)
I found it in a used book. Somebody had already underlined it.
He meant the study of Torah. I'm a guest in that sentence.
Here's how I borrow it. / We don't have to finish it. / We just don't get to quit.
Nearly there. I usually walk this block on my own. / Just me and one line from an old Norse poem.
Rich did I feel when a comrade I found. (the Hávamál, stanza 47, in Bellows's translation; quoted exactly, the poem not named aloud)
That's the poem talking. / Mostly.
This is me. / They'll have started without me.
Should you come up? / even with the food of immortality on your table, you don't eat while a guest stands outside. / So you see my position.
Come on up.
You're late. Nobody has started.
I counted you in twice.
You took the long way. / I had company.
Chair.
The guest is served first. That is the rule. / It's my house. / It's still the rule.
And the ruling stands!
It's a crazy mixed up world out there. Keep the ones that make you feel sane close. (the owner's line)
Stay warm, folks. Goodnight. (the owner's line; a goodnight with a word for the audience before it)
devices: a whole episode that is one unbroken piece outside the studio, with no posts, no guests, no standing segments, no stock title card, no announcer and no audience sound

the open (the episode's one turned item, at the owner's word): the show's own logo, drawn by the studio's own function, alone and centred on black and fully lit from the first frame with no fade in, held in silence, then stuttering like a sign whose power has been cut (a clean cut to off, then on, half lit or off in short slots, off more and more often) to seven quiet dry ticks, and out; a second of black; then the studio switched off. It turns the way both aired episodes began, where the same logo came up in the first seconds and the show started
the lit logo as the first frame of the file, so that it is the picture a feed shows before the video plays; the logo is not drawn again anywhere in the episode, the credits included

the studio switched off and barely drawn, the sign and ON AIR dark and blank, one work lamp making a pool of light by the desk, the host alone in an overcoat looking down, silence, then his head coming up to us in the doorway and his first words, that there is no show tonight
the host off the air and out of costume: a long rumpled overcoat with the collar up, no tuxedo, no bow tie; a gold scarf put on by cutting to the collar as it settles; a cardigan at his own table
the camera as a person who walks beside the host: asked along, asked a question, answered, left on the pavement, let in, given a chair, served, and then not looked at
a listening hold: the host turns to the camera and nothing else in the picture changes for a second or two, where the viewer's question would be
a tracking walk, chest up, the host side-on with a bob a step and a puff of breath, a street sliding behind him in layers at different speeds, lamps drawn again upside down in a wet road
the host telling the state of the world on himself, in profile, without describing it: one sentence he keeps saying, meant two opposite ways
footsteps made from the band's percussion voices as lip pops in music blocks, two tracks a little out of step, soft in snow
a restaurant seen from the pavement: a big window, silhouettes at every table bobbing, a small neon OPEN, and a lit kitchen hatch at the back with one cook, a plate on the pass and steam
a silhouette that does what a spoken story says on the word: the cook stops and leans in on slows down, then works slowly while the room goes on at full speed, and nothing is said for three seconds
a busker under a lamp with an empty open case and nobody listening, heard before he is seen, singing a wordless tune with no caption and a small note glyph by his head
a tune that stops one note short, a held silence, a coin that arcs in from below the frame and lands with a click, and the tune starting again behind us after we have walked on

a pedestrian sign as the scene: DON'T WALK in red on an empty road, its red on the host in close-up while he quotes, still red for three seconds after he has finished, then WALK in green on one tick, on no word, with nobody looking at it
a side street at the crossing whose lamps recede to one plain building that closes it, so that nothing far shows through
the only words on screen in the whole piece: the logo's own (THE LATE CLUSTER, with Larry Nx) for under three seconds at the top, then OPEN, DON'T WALK and WALK; a blank envelope, unnamed shopfronts
a quotation from a named translation spoken plainly in close-up in two beats at its comma, followed by silence, with its source in the credits and not on screen
true silence as a place: no sound at all between the lines for fifty seconds at a kerb
snow that starts halfway across a road in a stretch with no words and never stops; flakes past the window of the last room

one old line said to the road and half taken back: the host owns up to a line of an old poem he walks the last block with, says it by heart looking straight ahead with only footsteps under it, glances at the camera to see whether he was heard, says it was the poem talking, and a step later adds Mostly
a cut, not a push, to a closer profile of the host for a quoted line, and a cut back on his glance; no word on screen for the line, the poem not named aloud and its speaker not named at all
a line said looking straight ahead, then a glance at the camera and away again at once

the host's building as a brick front with one warm crowded top window, a figure standing at it who is gone before the street door is let open from upstairs; warm light falling across the snow and the host
a close shot of a lit window from the street while the host tells an old couplet about a table and a guest
two cuts that jump the walk forward, so that a place is behind us or already in view when the next thing happens
a see-through head: the street shows through the host's wireframe head, with no black fill behind it

the house cast off duty in their own clothes and their own hues at one long table that hides them below the chest: no jackets, no crest, no headset; the announcer at the head in an open wooden chair, seated inside the table's far corner so that the tabletop is really in front of what it hides
a chair in the host's gold kept empty on the near side of the table with its back to us
all six heads turning from the host to the camera and holding for two seconds in a room whose light does not change, then one word (Chair.)
a second chair sliding in beside the host's; the camera going to it and settling at table height; a plate, a glass and a fork sliding in along the bottom of the frame
a covered dish that is uncovered after a cut, with steam, never named
a served bowl that is never seen to move: it stands at the host's left with his head turned to it, and after a cut it is at the viewer's plate with his look on it, so it has gone past him
the announcer at her plate through the host's objection, then lifting her head and looking at him, level and unhurried, to hold her ruling
the welcome as being ignored: after the viewer is served, every shot is from the viewer's seat, nothing moves along the table, and nobody at it looks at the camera
one friend's laugh as a voiced line with no caption, in place of any audience sound

a room of friends as layered murmur: a loud burst and a gasp as the door opens, near silence for a look, then a bed that drops back when the host turns to the camera and runs unbroken under his last lines and for five seconds after the last word
the close: the host turns from the table to the camera for three plain lines, nods, turns back to his friends; three seconds from the viewer's chair; a fade to black

plain black credit cards after the fade: the show's name as plain text, the house cast by role, an invented busker listed as On the corner, the two translations quoted and the two works told from, and the line that every voice is synthesized; no studio, no logo, no goodnight heading, no applause
